skill.name: Author fingerprints: what makes one author's style different
skill.why: Every author has a style, like a fingerprint. Spot it and you'll know them.
skill.how: Look at sentence length, word choices and jokes. Then ask: who writes like that?

beats.say: Every author leaves fingerprints: habits in how they write.
Some authors write short sentences. They feel fast and tense.
Some write long sentences, packed with colour and detail.
beats.show: The **silver, sleepy** sea **rolled up the sand like a cat stretching in the sun**.

beats.say: And some can't get through one line without a joke.
beats.show: The pirate was so old, **his parrot had grown a beard**.

beats.say: Those habits are the author's style. Spot them to name the author.

weDo.text: Dash Kettle writes thrillers. This is how his newest book starts: 'The lights went out. Silence. Then footsteps. Close.'
weDo.prompt: Which line could Dash Kettle have written next?
weDo.hint: Look at how long Dash's sentences are, and whether he jokes.
weDo.success: Short, tense sentences, and no jokes. That's Dash Kettle's fingerprint.

options.text: The old green door, peeling and tired, swung shut with a long, sad sigh.
options.reason: That's long and slow, full of detail. Dash writes short and fast.

options.text: A door slammed. Then nothing.
The door shut. (Doors are rude like that.)
options.reason: That's a joke. Dash never jokes. He keeps it tense.

weDo.success: Short and tense, long and colourful, or jokey. Each style is a different author's fingerprint.

encounters.frame: A page with no cover blew into Narra the Teller's cave. The Scrittle sniffed it.
encounters.text: Midnight. The cave was cold. Drip. Drip. Drip. Kit held her torch tight. Something moved in the dark. She froze. A shape. Big. Wet. Coming closer. Her torch flickered. Then it died. Kit ran. She did not look back. She did not stop. Her feet slapped the wet rock. Slap. Slap. Slap. The way out was close now. Ten steps. Five. Behind her, something laughed. Then the laughing stopped. And the footsteps began.

encounters.success: Tiny sentences, sound words like 'Drip' and a scary ending. That's Dash Kettle's fingerprint.

encounters.text: The morning tide slid up the beach like a sheet of pale green glass. Ella walked slowly along the shore. Shells lay scattered everywhere, pink and cream and the soft grey of a dove's wing. A crab, as red as a ripe tomato, scuttled sideways into a rock pool. The pool was very still. Inside it, tiny fish flickered like sparks from a campfire, silver and gold and gone in a blink. Ella knelt down. She stayed there for an hour, watching the light dance on the water like a thousand tiny mirrors. By then the sun was high, and her knees were sandy and sore.

encounters.text: The crab stopped. Listened. Sand hissed in the wind. Then a shadow. Huge. Above. The seagull dived. The crab ran. Left. Right. Left again. Its claws were snapping. The burrow was close. Twenty steps. Ten. Five. Sand flew. Its legs ached. The seagull's beak struck the sand. Thunk. Missed. The crab dived into the burrow. Safe. For now. It waited in the dark. One minute. Two. Nothing. Slowly, it peeked out. One eye. Then two. The beach was empty. Too empty. The wind had stopped. The waves had stopped. Even the seagull was gone. Then the sand beside the burrow began to move.

encounters.frame: A dusty book with no cover was found in the Twotide lighthouse. The Scrittle won't go near it.
encounters.text: The old lighthouse stood at the edge of the atoll like a tall grey ghost. Its paint peeled away in long, curling strips, the colour of old bones. Inside, the spiral staircase wound upwards into the gloom, every step furred with dust as soft as moth wings. Cobwebs hung from the railings like grey lace curtains, trembling at every breath of air. Far below, the sea sighed against the rocks, as slow as a sleeping giant. Ada climbed slowly, her lantern throwing a trembling circle of honey-coloured light against the walls. Somewhere above her, the wind sang through a broken window, as thin and sad as someone humming a half-forgotten lullaby. At the top, the great lamp sat in its cage of brass and glass, cold and dark and patient. It seemed to have been waiting fifty years for someone to come. Ada reached out a hand that shook like a leaf in the wind. And then, as slowly as a flower opening, the great lamp began to glow.

encounters.frame: The Echobat brought Narra a page from a sea thriller. Who else writes like this?
encounters.text: Extract A. Night. The boat rocked. Sam woke up. The clock said 3:12. Then 3:13. Something was wrong. Too quiet. No engine. No waves. He sat up. The cabin was cold. His breath made clouds. He found his boots. Wet. Why were they wet? He climbed on deck. Fog. Thick. Grey. He couldn't see the front of the boat. He couldn't see his hand. Then a sound. Splash. Close. Very close. His heart thumped. Thump. Thump. Sam grabbed the torch. Click. Nothing. Click. Still nothing. Dead battery. Another splash. Closer now. Something bumped the side of the boat. Once. Twice. The boat tipped. Sam held the rail. His knuckles went white. 'Hello?' he whispered. His voice shook. No answer. Just water. Dripping. Then a hand. Wet. Cold. It gripped the rail beside his. Sam didn't move. He couldn't. He didn't even blink. Slowly, a head rose out of the water. And it smiled.

encounters.frame: Narra the Teller's apprentice is learning to write like Dash Kettle. The Scrittle is marking the homework.
encounters.text: This is how Dash Kettle starts his cooking thriller, Hot Pot: 'The kitchen was dark. One light. One pot. Mo lifted the lid. Steam. Hiss. Something inside moved. He dropped the lid. Clang. Silence. Then the pot began to rattle. Faster. Louder. Mo backed away. The door was locked.' The apprentice was asked to rewrite this sentence by Marigold Featherby so that it sounds like Dash: 'The great silver pot bubbled and burped on the stove like a grumpy little volcano, puffing clouds of white steam that drifted lazily across the yellow kitchen.' Narra told the apprentice to look closely at how Dash writes: how long his sentences are, which sounds he uses and how he makes you feel. The apprentice wrote four different versions. Narra says only one of them sounds like Dash Kettle. The other three still sound like somebody else, or like nobody at all. The Scrittle has already drawn a gold star next to one of them.

encounters.frame: A battered paperback floated down from Maxx's drone onto Twotide Atoll. The author's name has been scratched off.
encounters.text: Captain Lulu Snodgrass had been in charge of the starship Crumpet for exactly four minutes when the first thing went wrong. (It was a new record. The old record was six minutes, and that was also Lulu.) Outside the window, the planet Zorb hung in space, a vast swirl of violet and emerald clouds that rolled slowly across its surface like paint stirred into a tin of cream. It was, everyone agreed, the most beautiful planet in the galaxy. It was also the smelliest. Nobody had told Lulu that part. As the Crumpet drifted closer, the stink seeped in through the air vents, a thick, eggy, cabbagey, sock-drawer sort of smell that made the ship's cat faint dramatically onto the control panel. (The cat was fine. The control panel was not.) Lights flashed. Alarms howled. The Crumpet began to spin. 'Do something!' shouted the first officer, a nervous robot called Kevin who was mostly made of old toasters. Lulu did something. She opened a window. (Never open a window in space. I cannot stress this enough. Write it on your hand.) Luckily, the Crumpet's windows had been installed upside down, so instead of everybody being sucked out into space, the stink was sucked out instead. Lulu was awarded a medal for quick thinking. She accepted it with great dignity, then tripped over the cat on her way off the stage.

encounters.frame: Narra the Teller made notes comparing two authors' accounts of the Twotide Brass Band concert. One part is wrong.
encounters.text: Extract A. The band played as the sun went down, and the music rose over the harbour like warm smoke, curling between the masts of the fishing boats and drifting out across the water. The trumpets shone like polished gold in the last of the light, and the big bass drum kept time as steadily as a slow, contented heartbeat. Out on the jetty, an old man closed his eyes and swayed, as gently as seagrass in the tide. Children sat along the edge, their bare feet dangling over the water like fishing lines. When the final note faded, the whole harbour seemed to hold its breath. Extract B. The Twotide Brass Band played at sunset, which was brave of them, because the tuba player had eaten three meat pies beforehand. (I'm not saying the tuba sounded different. I'm just saying the seagulls left.) The drummer, a man called Big Trev, hit the drum so enthusiastically that his hat flew off and landed on a pelican. The pelican kept it. Then, during the quiet bit, the tuba let out a noise that I can only describe as WHOOOMPH. A dog howled. A baby applauded. Everybody agreed it was the best concert in years. (The pelican still wears the hat on Sundays.)

encounters.success: Both extracts really do describe the same sunset concert. Marigold uses no brackets at all; that's only Bunny's habit.

encounters.frame: A fan sent Narra the Teller a chapter 'by Dash Kettle'. The Scrittle thinks it's a fake.
encounters.text: Midnight. The harbour was still. Too still. Detective Rook stood on the jetty. Waiting. Watching. The fog rolled in. Thick. Grey. Like porridge, but less tasty. Somewhere, a boat creaked. His coat was wet. His shoes were wet. Even his sandwich was wet. Soggy. Like his career. Rook ate it anyway. Detectives can't be fussy. He checked his watch. Five past twelve. The smuggler was late. Smugglers were always late. It was the one thing you could count on, apart from their terrible fashion sense. A sound. Footsteps. Rook spun around. Nothing. Just a seagull. It glared at him. He glared back. The seagull won. Then a light flickered out on the water. Once. Twice. Three times. The signal. Rook crouched behind a stack of crates. Clang. A boat bumped the jetty. A figure climbed out. Tall. Thin. Carrying a box. A moustache. Fake. Badly glued. Rook's heart pounded. This was it. Six months of work. He jumped out. 'Freeze!' The figure froze. The box fell. It burst open on the jetty. Fish fingers. Hundreds of them. Rook stared. The smuggler stared. 'They're for my nan,' said the smuggler. Rook sighed. It was going to be a long night. Then, behind them both, the water began to bubble.
encounters.prompt: The fan was trying to sound like Dash Kettle. What gives it away as a fake?
encounters.success: The jokes give it away: porridge fog, smugglers' fashion, a seagull winning a staring contest. Dash never jokes.

encounters.frame: Zed found two extracts in the Twotide library. Narra the Teller says the same author wrote both.
encounters.text: Extract A. The arcade blazed with light the moment Ruby pushed through the door, a dazzling jumble of pink and lime and electric blue that fizzed across the ceiling like lemonade poured too fast. Every machine sang its own bright, bubbling song, and the air smelled sweetly of popcorn and warm plastic. Ruby wandered between the rows of games as if she were walking through a garden in full bloom, her pocket heavy with coins that jingled like tiny bells. In the far corner, a claw machine full of plush toys glowed like an aquarium of sleepy, fluffy fish. Extract B. On the last day before the old game shop closed for good, the shelves stood bare and grey, like the ribs of a ship left to rot on the beach. Faded posters peeled from the walls like old sunburnt skin. Dust drifted through the single beam of afternoon light as slowly as snow falling in a dream. Mr Tan sat behind the counter, polishing a cartridge that nobody would ever buy, his face as tired and crumpled as an old paper bag. When Ruby walked in, he looked up, smiled a small, sad smile, and slid the cartridge across the counter to her without a word.
encounters.prompt: Which shared feature is an author's fingerprint?
encounters.success: Lemonade, tiny bells, a ship's ribs, a paper bag: both extracts are built from long sentences full of colourful comparisons.
